seoDescription: Learn the essential Java Data Transfer Object (DTO) pattern to build secure and maintainable APIs. This tutorial explains why you should not expose your database entities directly to the client and how DTOs provide a solution. Discover how to control the data your API sends, preventing sensitive information like passwords from being exposed. Through a practical Spring Boot example, you'll see how to create a CustomerDTO, write a custom mapper to transform your Customer entity, and refactor your service and controller layers.

chapters.title: Introduction and Course Promotion
chapters.description: The video introduces the Java DTO pattern and promotes an upcoming full-stack course and a giveaway for JetBrains IDEs.

chapters.title: Conceptual Overview of the DTO Pattern
chapters.description: This chapter provides a high-level explanation of the Data Transfer Object (DTO) pattern and its benefits.

chapters.title: Demonstrating the Problem with an API
chapters.description: An example API call is used to show the security risk of exposing entire database entities, including hashed passwords.

chapters.title: Creating the Customer DTO Record
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to create a new CustomerDTO class using a Java record to define the fields exposed to the client.

chapters.title: Implementing Mapping Logic in the Service
chapters.description: The controller and service are updated to use the new DTO, and the mapping logic is implemented directly in the service using a Java stream.

chapters.title: Refactoring to a Dedicated Mapper Class
chapters.description: To improve code structure, the mapping logic is extracted into a dedicated `CustomerDTOMapper` class that implements a Function interface.

chapters.title: Updating Unit Tests for the DTO
chapters.description: This part covers how to update the unit tests to reflect the changes in the service layer's return type and dependencies.

chapters.title: Verifying the Final API Response
chapters.description: The application is restarted, and Postman is used to verify that the API now correctly returns the controlled DTO without sensitive data.

chapters.title: DTOs for Input and Advanced Use Cases
chapters.description: The video discusses how DTOs are also useful for handling client input and for combining data from multiple entities into a single response.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Final Call to Action
chapters.description: The video concludes by summarizing the topic and encouraging viewers to like the video, enter the giveaway, and stay tuned for the new course.

## Conceptual Overview of the DTO Pattern

Without further ado, let's kick off this video. Cool. So DTO stands for Data Transfer Object. And the idea is that in your database, you might have models such as Customer, which has name, password, also a Car, which has brand, price, and a bunch of other fields in here. So here I'm actually limiting the fields for illustration purposes. And these entities right here, they are stored in a database.

Now the idea of the DTO pattern is that you have a mapper in here. So this mapper is responsible for performing data transformation from one data type to another. Now here the data type. So basically, if you want to send, for example, the customer information to your client that consumes the API, it's not really feasible for you to send the password, right? So you would never do that. And if you do, trust me, you're going to be in trouble, right? So what you do is you have the mapper. And this mapper will basically take maybe the customer as well as the car, and it will perform a transformation, meaning that it will take the information or the properties and then transform it into a data type, or in this case, a class called Customer DTO, where here you have full control of what fields you expose to your API. So the client, when it sends an Http request, for example, it's not aware of the internals of your system, all it gets is whatever you have exposed, hence data transfer object.

Now, the beauty of this is that you can build different views from your domain models. So in here, so if you have a bunch of other classes in here that you basically want to send to your client. So one Http request, then another one for getting the car, then another one for getting transactions, another one for getting the address. So you can see four Http requests. What you do instead is you basically bundle everything into one request, and the customer or the DTO model takes care of that. So basically you can build different views of your domain models as well as reduce the number of calls.
